newsitem.title: USA: Dollar bolstered by U.S. rate rise, weak Japanese yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar bolstered by U.S. rate rise, weak Japanese yen.

text.p: The dollar rose against most major currencies Tuesday, bolstered by an increase in short-term interest rates by the Federal Reserve and fresh signs Japan will keep rates low.

At its regularly scheduled meeting, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) boosted its overnight federal funds lending rate target, for the first time since Feb. 1, 1995, by a quarter percentage point to 5.50 percent. The federal funds rate is the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans.
Higher interest rates tend to lift the dollar by making dollar-denominated assets worth more.
The increase matched financial market expectations but caused the dollar to briefly drop then rise against the German mark in sporadic trading.
Soon after, the dollar later gave up some of its gains as stock and bond markets turned decidedly negative.

"The dollar is clearly the tail rather than the dog here. It's following the reaction in U.S. asset markets," said Ben Strauss, an assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer and Co. Strauss described dollar trade just after the Fed announcement as "very choppy".
The dollar rose to 1.6903 marks by the end of trade from 1.6880 at Monday's close and to 123.70 Japanese yen from 122.85.
The Dow Jones industrials and 30-year U.S. Treasury bond shed morning gains after the Fed announcement and closed lower, pulling the dollar from its session highs.
"The Fed rate hike was as expected and the currency market behaved as expected," said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank in Chicago.

"People initially bought dollars on the perception of higher U.S. interest rates, but upon further inspection most of the market had already priced in that move and later we moved with other U.S. asset markets," he added.

Earlier, the dollar rose against the Japanese yen after the Bank of Japan allowed the overnight call rate, a short-term money market rate, to dip to an average of 0.53 percentage point from 0.57 percentage point on Monday.
The dollar also was helped by comments from a top Japanese banker who said Japanese interest rates will remain low for some time.
Shunsaku Hashimoto, head of the Federation of Bankers' Associations of Japan, said Japanese monetary policy would become more flexible in the second half of the fiscal year ending March 31, 1998.
The comment caused the mark to surge against the yen, pulling the dollar higher against the yen as well.

In other trading, the dollar rose to 1.4655 Swiss francs from 1.4584 Monday, but fell to Canadian $1.3782 from C$1.3795. Britain's pound was nearly flat after a sharp rally Monday, closing at $1.6195.
